questions.question: What is retrieval-augmented generation, or RAG?
questions.answer: RAG retrieves relevant material from an approved source collection and provides it to a language model when generating an answer. It can help an assistant answer questions about your own information, but retrieval quality, access controls and evaluation still matter.

questions.question: What is MCP development?
questions.answer: Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a shared interface for AI applications to connect to tools and data. We build MCP servers in Python around your approved APIs or systems, define the tools and resources they expose, handle authorisation with OAuth and managed secrets, and test them with the intended compatible clients. Access permissions and approval requirements remain part of the application design.

questions.question: Can an AI agent query our databases safely?
questions.answer: It can, when access is engineered rather than prompted. In practice that means a connector or MCP server that authenticates as a scoped service identity, exposes only approved tables or endpoints, generates SQL against a governed reporting layer, validates the query and the result before returning it, and logs every call. Whitelists and read-only access keep an agent away from anything it has no business touching.

questions.question: Do we need to train our own AI model?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. The right scope may use an existing model with retrieval and application integration. We review your use case, data, evaluation criteria and operating constraints before proposing an approach.

questions.question: Can the assistant respect different user permissions?
questions.answer: Role-aware access can be part of the scope. The design must enforce authorisation before protected data is retrieved or an action is performed; instructions written into a prompt are not a substitute for application access controls.

questions.question: What determines the cost of an AI assistant?
questions.answer: The main factors are source preparation, integrations, permission rules, evaluation, user interface and support. Ongoing costs also depend on model usage, retrieval infrastructure and traffic. These should be considered alongside the build estimate.

questions.question: What is an MCP server, in practice?
questions.answer: It is a small service that describes a set of tools and resources in a standard way, so any compatible AI application can use them without a bespoke integration. In practice it is ordinary backend engineering: authenticate, validate the input, call the underlying system, shape the response, log the call. The protocol is the straightforward part; the access model is the work.

questions.question: How is this different from your AI automation and RAG service?
questions.answer: The AI automation, RAG and MCP development page covers the assistant itself: knowledge sources, retrieval, model behaviour and the user-facing workflow. This page covers the layer underneath it — the servers and connectors that give agents governed access to live systems. Many projects need both and they are often scoped together. If you are not sure which one you are asking for, describe the workflow and we will say.

questions.question: Can an agent be allowed to write data, not just read it?
questions.answer: It can, with deliberate design. Write tools are kept separate from read tools, restricted to specific objects and operations, made idempotent where possible, and in most cases placed behind a human approval step that happens outside the model’s control. We would start read-only, prove tool selection is reliable, then add write capability one operation at a time.

questions.question: Which AI platforms can use what you build?
questions.answer: Any MCP-compatible client, which now covers the major assistant and IDE products, plus platform-specific connectors and plugins where an organisation has standardised on one vendor. We test against the clients you actually use, because a tool description that works well in one client can be read differently in another.

questions.question: How do you stop prompt injection turning a tool into a problem?
questions.answer: By not relying on the model to enforce anything. Permissions are checked server-side before a tool runs, tools expose only approved objects, generated SQL is validated against a whitelist, destructive operations are either not exposed or require human approval, and retrieved content is treated as data rather than as instructions. Logging every call means an unexpected request is visible afterwards, not merely prevented in theory.

questions.question: How much does custom MCP server development cost?
questions.answer: We quote after a scoping call, and terms are agreed per engagement. The recommended starting point is small: one server, one system, one small group of users and the three or four tools that cover most of their requests. MV.tech is a remote-first team based in Ahmedabad, India, with a lean model that avoids large-consultancy overhead.

questions.question: How do you connect Claude or another AI assistant to our database safely?
questions.answer: Instead of handing the assistant the keys, it calls an MCP server that runs under a scoped service identity against an approved set of tables, read-only by default and whitelisted rather than blocklisted. Where the agent generates SQL, the query is parsed and checked before it runs, with permitted objects only, row and cost limits and no writes, and results are validated before they are returned. Every call is logged with the caller, tool, time and outcome, and we test against real requests, including ones the server should refuse, before access is widened.

questions.question: Can you work with our existing Power BI model instead of rebuilding it?
questions.answer: Usually yes, and that is where we prefer to start. A review covers grain, relationships, calculated columns, duplicated measures, storage mode and refresh behaviour, and produces a written list of what to fix in place and what genuinely needs rebuilding. A rebuild is something we have to justify, not a starting assumption.

questions.question: What is a semantic model and why does it matter?
questions.answer: It is the layer between your warehouse and your dashboards that holds tables, relationships and agreed measures. When it exists, every report calculates revenue the same way. When it does not, each dashboard re-implements the logic and the numbers drift apart. It also lets analysts build their own views without writing joins.

questions.question: Our dashboards disagree with each other. Where does that get fixed?
questions.answer: Almost always upstream of the dashboard. The usual causes are different filters, a different grain, different date logic or a metric defined twice. We trace each figure back to its source, agree one definition per metric with a named owner, and move the calculation into the model so a report is no longer the place the logic lives.

questions.question: Which BI tool should we use?
questions.answer: Whichever one your team will maintain. Power BI suits organisations already in Microsoft 365 that need a governed semantic layer; Tableau suits heavy visual exploration; Looker Studio is reasonable for lighter reporting over Google Cloud data; Streamlit fits when the output is really an interactive Python tool. We would rather improve the tool you have than sell you a migration.

questions.question: Do we need a data warehouse before we can do BI properly?
questions.answer: Not always, but usually. A semantic model can read an operational database for a while and sometimes that is the right call. Once reports need history, several sources, or a grain the source system does not store, a curated warehouse layer costs less than repeatedly patching reports. We can tell you which situation you are in after looking at the sources.

questions.question: Our dashboard refresh is too slow or times out. What can be done?
questions.answer: The fix is to reduce what the report has to read rather than importing less data as a workaround. That means partitioning, incremental refresh, aggregation tables, pushing transformation back into the warehouse and removing columns nothing uses. On past work this has reduced query scan sizes by 60 to 75% and moved refreshes from hours to minutes.

questions.question: How long does a data warehouse migration take?
questions.answer: It depends far more on dependencies than on data volume. Discovery and dependency analysis on a mid-sized estate typically takes weeks; the migration is then scoped domain by domain, each reconciled before the next begins. We would rather give an estimate after discovery than before it, and discovery can be bought as a standalone piece of work.

questions.question: How do you prove the new warehouse is correct?
questions.answer: By comparing it with the old one, automatically and repeatedly. Record counts and control totals per load, date coverage and gap checks, null and duplicate profiles, key uniqueness, and metric-level comparison of reported figures. Every difference is investigated and then either fixed or documented as a deliberate change, including the cases where the legacy number turns out to be the wrong one.

questions.question: Can we migrate without breaking existing dashboards?
questions.answer: That is what the dependency analysis is for. Before anything moves we trace which reports, extracts and semantic models read which objects, and flag the business logic hiding inside them. Dashboards are then repointed and reconciled visual by visual, usually while both platforms run in parallel, so the old estate is switched off only after the new numbers have been signed off.

questions.question: Should we lift and shift, or redesign?
questions.answer: Usually a mix, decided per domain. Lifting and shifting is faster and keeps reconciliation simple, but it carries forward the modelling problems and often the cost profile. Redesigning is right where the grain is wrong, where legacy logic is unmaintainable, or where query patterns will change on the new platform. Discovery is what tells you which objects belong in which category.

questions.question: Our reporting lives in spreadsheets rather than a database. Is that still a migration?
questions.answer: Yes, and it is a common one. The shape of the work is the same: find the sources behind the spreadsheets, document the rules that live in formulas and in people’s heads, model them in the warehouse and reconcile the output against the last few months of manual figures. The difference is that more of the discovery happens in conversation than in the information schema.

questions.question: How much does a data warehouse migration cost?

Discovery can be bought as a standalone piece of work, and migrating one reporting domain first gives an estimate for the rest of the estate based on your data rather than on a template. Commercial terms are agreed per engagement.

The migration runs on written work both sides can review: a source-to-target mapping that both sides sign off, automated reconciliation results at every stage, and written sign-off per domain before legacy objects are retired. questions.question: Why not just use a public chain dataset?
questions.answer: Public datasets are a reasonable starting point for common chains and standard token transfers. They tend to fall short on newer or smaller networks, on contracts whose events are not standard, and on the business layer: your token registry, your categorisation rules, your reporting currency and your reconciliation against internal records. We use public datasets where they fit and build ingestion where they do not.

questions.question: How do you handle a contract with no published ABI?
questions.answer: Several ways, in order of preference: a verified ABI from the explorer, a standard interface the contract conforms to, an ABI supplied by whoever deployed it, or reconstruction from method signatures and observed event topics. Whichever route is used, the decoding rules are recorded per contract and the raw input data is retained, so decoding can be corrected and replayed without re-ingesting the chain.

questions.question: Can analysts correct a figure without breaking the audit trail?
questions.answer: That is what the override layer is for. Base tables hold what the chain reported and are never edited. Corrections, whitelists and manual classifications live in separate tables with an author, a timestamp and a reason, and are applied when the reporting view is built. Both the original and the adjusted figure stay available, which is usually what an auditor asks to see.

questions.question: How do you value tokens that barely trade?
questions.answer: Carefully, and visibly. The valuation method is a documented rule per token: reference price at block timestamp, a defined source hierarchy, a fallback, or explicitly no valuation at all. Unvalued volume is reported rather than hidden. It is better for a finance team to see that a share of activity has no reliable price than to receive a confident number built on a thin market.

questions.question: Can this feed our existing warehouse and dashboards?
questions.answer: Yes. On-chain data is just another source: it lands in the same layered warehouse, under the same validation and modelling standards, and is read by Power BI, Looker Studio, Tableau or a Streamlit tool alongside everything else. Teams usually want it joined to off-chain records — customers, internal accounts, fiat movements — and that join is where most of the analytical value appears.

questionsHeading: Questions people ask before hiring a BigQuery consultant.

questions.question: How much does BigQuery consulting cost?
questions.answer: We quote after a scoping call. The estimate depends on the number of sources, the volume of history to load, how much SQL needs translating, the reports in scope and whether you want support after handover. A first project is scoped to be verifiable in weeks, and the quote for anything beyond it is based on your own query history.

questions.question: Why is our BigQuery bill so high?
questions.answer: Usually because queries read more than they need to. The common causes are tables with no partitioning, dashboards that query raw tables, scheduled queries that rebuild full history every hour and SELECT * in views that other views build on. The fix starts with the job history, which shows exactly which queries bill the most bytes and who runs them, and then applies partition filters, clustering, materialised views and per-user limits in that order.

questions.question: Should we partition BigQuery tables by ingestion time or by an event date column?
questions.answer: By the column your queries filter on, which is usually an event or transaction date. Ingestion-time partitioning is simpler to load but only helps when reports ask about when data arrived, which they rarely do. Where late-arriving records are common, the load uses MERGE into the correct date partition rather than appending to today's, and a partition-filter requirement stops anyone scanning the full table by accident.

questions.question: Can you migrate us to BigQuery from SQL Server, PostgreSQL, Redshift or Snowflake?
questions.answer: Yes. The work starts with discovery of what exists and what depends on it, then a source-to-target mapping per object, SQL translated and tested, and reconciliation of counts, totals and reported metrics at each layer before the old platform is switched off. Platform-specific SQL, stored procedures and cross-database joins are the usual blockers, and they are found in discovery rather than at cutover.

questions.question: Can a remote team in India run our BigQuery project?

MV.tech works from Ahmedabad, India, and agrees a collaboration window in your timezone before the engagement starts, which typically covers UK and European business hours, US Eastern mornings, Gulf hours or Asia-Pacific afternoons. Access is through your own Google Cloud project with IAM roles you grant and can revoke, logs stay in your project and no credentials are needed for an initial enquiry.

questions.question: Is Looker Studio good enough, or do we need Power BI?
questions.answer: Looker Studio is reasonable for reporting over BigQuery when the model lives in the warehouse and the reports read curated views. Power BI becomes the better choice when you need a governed semantic layer, row-level security or complex measures, or when the organisation already runs on Microsoft 365. Either way the metric definitions belong in BigQuery, so changing the reporting tool later is a repointing exercise rather than a rebuild.

questionsHeading: Questions about hiring a Power BI consultant.

questions.question: Why is my Power BI dashboard refresh slow?
questions.answer: Usually because the model imports more than it reads, or does work at refresh time that belongs in the warehouse. The common causes are calculated columns over large fact tables, high-cardinality columns such as timestamps or free text, Power Query steps that stop folding so a whole table is pulled before it is filtered, and a full refresh where an incremental policy would do. We profile the model with DAX Studio and the refresh history first, then change the few things that account for most of the time.

questions.question: What is a Power BI semantic model?
questions.answer: It is the dataset layer between your warehouse and your reports: tables, relationships, measures, hierarchies and security roles. When it exists as one governed model, every report calculates revenue the same way and analysts can build their own views without writing joins. When each report carries its own copy of the data and its own measures, the numbers drift apart.

questions.question: Can you fix our existing Power BI model instead of rebuilding it?
questions.answer: Usually, and that is the cheaper place to start. The review covers grain, relationships, calculated columns, duplicated measures, storage mode and refresh behaviour, and ends in a written list of what to fix in place and what genuinely needs remodelling. A rebuild is something we have to justify, not a starting assumption.

questions.question: Can you migrate our SSAS or Azure Analysis Services model to Power BI?
questions.answer: Yes. The first step is documenting what the tabular model contains and which reports depend on each table and measure, because that decides whether it can move largely as-is through the XMLA endpoint or should be remodelled. Measures are compared old against new on identical filters before any report is repointed, and both models run in parallel until the figures are signed off.

questions.question: How much does Power BI consulting cost?
questions.answer: We quote after a scoping call. The estimate depends on the number of reports and sources, the state of the existing model, whether an Analysis Services migration is involved and how much reconciliation the business needs to see. A review of one existing model is a bounded piece of work and is usually the cheapest way to find out what the rest would involve.

questions.question: How do you prove the numbers on a report are right?
questions.answer: By reconciling them to source and keeping the check running. Record counts, control totals and date coverage per table, plus the handful of figures people actually act on, are compared against the source system on every refresh. Differences are investigated and either fixed or written down as a deliberate change, which sometimes means the old report was the one that was wrong.
